reason: Multiple independent sources corroborate extensive details about WASP-12b's asphalt-dark albedo, tidal egg-like distortion, atmospheric stripping, and measured orbital decay.
story: In 2008, astronomers discovered WASP-12b, a scorching gas giant orbiting just two million miles from its host star. It whips around the star in roughly twenty-six hours, but gravity has turned this world into a nightmare. Tidal forces pull the planet into a deformed egg shape while ripping its superheated atmosphere into space. Even stranger, Hubble observations revealed WASP-12b is pitch black, darker than fresh asphalt. Because dayside temperatures soar past 4,600 degrees Fahrenheit, atmospheric molecules are torn apart, leaving no reflective cloud decks. Instead, the planet traps over 94 percent of starlight, glowing red from sheer thermal radiation. Worst of all, its clock is speeding up. Precise transit timings show WASP-12b's year shrinks by roughly 30 milliseconds annually as tidal friction drains its orbital energy. Locked in an irreversible death spiral, this pitch-black world has only about three million years left before being utterly consumed.
angle: WASP-12b is darker than fresh asphalt, absorbing over 94% of starlight while being stretched into an egg and eaten alive by its parent star.

claims.claim: WASP-12b was discovered in 2008 by the SuperWASP / WASP transit survey.
WASP-12b is a hot Jupiter gas giant exoplanet.
The planet orbits approximately 2 million miles (roughly 3.5 million kilometers) from its host star.
WASP-12b completes one full orbit in roughly 1.1 Earth days (about 26 hours).
WASP-12b is tidally locked to its host star, keeping one side in permanent day and the other in permanent night.
Enormous tidal forces from the parent star have distorted WASP-12b into an egg shape (prolate spheroid).
WASP-12b reflects less than 6.4% of incoming light, making it darker than fresh asphalt.
The exoplanet traps at least 94% of the visible starlight falling into its atmosphere.
Dayside temperatures on WASP-12b reach extreme highs of roughly 4,600 to 4,700 °F (over 2,500 K).
The dayside atmosphere is so hot that molecules are thermally broken down, preventing reflective clouds from forming.
Despite reflecting almost no light, the planet is so hot that it glows red like molten metal.
The planet's superheated atmosphere is overflowing its Roche lobe and actively spilling onto the host star.
Hubble's Cosmic Origins Spectrograph detected the planet's atmospheric material escaping and being consumed by the star.
WASP-12b's orbital period is decaying, with transits arriving earlier each year by roughly 29 to 30 milliseconds.
Tidal interactions between the planet and star are draining orbital energy, causing WASP-12b to spiral inward.
Astronomers estimate the planet will be entirely consumed by its parent star in roughly 3 to 10 million years.
The planet has a mass roughly 1.4 to 1.5 times the mass of Jupiter.
WASP-12b is highly inflated, with a radius nearly twice that of Jupiter.

disputed: Distance from Earth: S2, S3, and S5 cite approximately 1,400 light-years, while S7 states 870 light-years. Script should omit the distance or attribute the modern 1,400 light-year figure.

Remaining lifetime: S1 and S4 note older estimates gave WASP-12b up to 10 million years, but recent studies refine the countdown to about 3 million years. Script should say: 'estimated between 3 and 10 million years, with recent studies pointing to just 3 million.'

Planet radius: S1 mentions the extended atmosphere reaches nearly three times Jupiter's radius, whereas S3, S5, S6, and S7 state the planet itself is 1.8 to 2 times Jupiter's radius. Clarify that the swollen planetary body is about twice Jupiter's size while the escaping gas envelope balloons even further.
